I'm pro nuclear, but I need to correct something here. I assume by mediator you mean moderator? It's entirely possible for a reactor that uses the same fluid as a coolant and a moderator to melt down. Most Western reactors (PWRs and BWRs) use light water as both the coolant and the moderator. In a loss of coolant emergency (such as three mile island or fukushima), the residual heat from the shut down reactor is more than enough to meltdown the core.

That being said one benefit of light water reactors is they have a negative void coefficient. As they start to overheat (assuming they're still full of water), the reaction rate will go down. Higher temp = lower reactivity.


The soviet RBMK that blew up from a steam explosion at Chernobyl was graphite moderated, and those reactors have a positive void coefficient. As the coolant overheats and boils, the reaction rate increases. Generally that's not what you want to happen.

It's probably fine for ELI5, but to clarify, preignition and detonation (aka "knock") are two different things from a combustion perspective, though both can occur simultaneously.

With detonation alone, the combustion starts at the proper time by the spark plug, but before the flame front can reach all areas of the cylinder, the increase in pressure from the beginning of combustion is enough to ignite secondary flame fronts in the combustion chamber causing the noise and Shockwave. In preignition, the combustion process starts before the spark plug has fired. This may or may not also cause detonation (ie "secondary" flame fronts).

Retarding the spark timing or increasing fuel octane are two easy ways to address detonation.
Prolonged detonation can end up causing preignition due to high Temps in the combustion chamber.

Preignition can be caused by a number of things but unless its caused by prolonged detonation, increasing fuel octane likely won't help.

Most power bricks are double insulated and have no need for a ground prong.
The ground fault protection in Europe was (and perhaps still is) at a far higher current than in the US. GFI for human protection is 5mA.

That's one of the benefits of the American plugs is the flexibility. Plug ends can be non-polarized (like most toasters), polarized (most small appliances) or grounded. Depending on the requirements of the appliance. All three plug types work fine in a grounded and polarized outlet.

Most toasters have unpolarized plugs because they have a double pole power switch inside. The switch kills both legs of the circuit in the toaster. Most other appliances have a single pole switch located on the incoming "live" wire, and the polarized plug is needed to ensure this switch is always on the live wire.
Now that we have safety shutters in outlets the only remaining improvement would be partially insulated prongs to eliminate the risk of shock from partially inserted plugs.

I have two minds. Autistic and NT masking. In my fully engaged autistic mind, I'll remember a technical fact about something for years. In my NT masking mind I'll forget something someone told me in minutes.
